task_3.title: Suppress PytestAssertRewriteWarning for pyproject.toml-based editable installs
task_3.description: When a pytest plugin is installed in editable mode using the pyproject.toml-based editable build mechanism introduced in pip 21.3, pytest's assertion rewrite machinery attempts to rewrite the `__editable__` finder modules that pip places in site-packages. Because these modules are already imported by the time pytest processes them, a spurious PytestAssertRewriteWarning is emitted. The fix excludes modules whose names start with `__editable__` from the set of rewritable modules, similar to how `setup` modules were already excluded.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that installing a pytest plugin in editable mode via `pip install -e .` using pyproject.toml-based builds (pip 21.3+) does not produce a spurious `PytestAssertRewriteWarning` about `__editable__` finder modules that cannot be rewritten.

expectation.grounded: The `_iter_rewritable_modules` function must skip any module whose name starts with `__editable__`, preventing these modules from being yielded as candidates for assertion rewriting. This means `PytestAssertRewriteWarning` will no longer be raised for editable-install finder modules. The existing exclusion of `setup` modules must remain intact.
expectation.conceptual: When pytest discovers installed plugin packages, it should silently ignore synthetic finder modules created by pip's editable-install mechanism. Users should see a clean test session output with no warnings related to editable installation internals.

constraints.grounded: The exclusion must apply only to modules whose names begin with the `__editable__` prefix. All other simple modules that were previously yielded by `_iter_rewritable_modules` must continue to be yielded. The existing `setup` module exclusion must not be altered. Legitimate plugin modules installed via editable mode must still be rewritten normally.
constraints.conceptual: The fix must be narrowly scoped to editable-install finder modules and must not suppress assertion rewriting for any user-authored or plugin-authored modules. Normal assertion rewriting behavior for all other modules must be preserved.

behavior: Modules with names starting with `__editable__` are excluded from the assertion rewrite candidate list produced by `_iter_rewritable_modules`.
The `PytestAssertRewriteWarning` for `__editable__` finder modules is no longer emitted during test session startup when editable-mode plugins are present.
The `setup` module exclusion continues to function as before.
All other plugin modules discovered from package metadata remain candidates for assertion rewriting.
acceptance_criteria: When a pytest plugin is installed in editable mode using pyproject.toml-based builds (pip 21.3+), running `pytest` produces no `PytestAssertRewriteWarning` mentioning `__editable__` modules.
When a pytest plugin is installed in editable mode, the plugin's actual modules are still subject to assertion rewriting as expected.
When a package includes a `setup.py`, the existing exclusion of the `setup` module from assertion rewriting still applies.
When `_iter_rewritable_modules` processes package file entries containing `__editable__` prefixed filenames, those entries are silently skipped and not yielded.
When a normal (non-editable) plugin is installed, its modules continue to be rewritten without any change in behavior.

task_1.title: Fix tearDown execution for class-level skipped unittest.TestCase under --pdb
task_1.description: When running pytest with the --pdb flag, unittest.TestCase classes decorated with unittest.skip or pytest.mark.skip at the class level still had their tearDown() method executed. This caused unexpected errors (e.g., NameError) and spurious PDB entry during tearDown for tests that should have been entirely skipped. The fix extends the existing skip detection to also check whether the enclosing test class is marked as skipped, not just the individual test method.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that when a unittest.TestCase class is decorated with unittest.skip (or pytest.mark.skip) at the class level and pytest is invoked with --pdb, the tearDown() method is NOT executed for any tests in that class. Previously, only method-level skip decorators were respected in this code path, causing class-level skipped tests to still run tearDown(), leading to unexpected errors and unwanted PDB sessions.

expectation.grounded: When TestCaseFunction prepares to run a unittest test under --pdb mode, the skip-detection logic (using _is_skipped) must check both the test method object (self.obj) and the parent UnitTestCase class object (self.parent.obj). If either is marked as skipped, tearDown() must be replaced with a no-op lambda so it is not invoked. The _explicit_tearDown attribute should not be set for class-level skipped tests, preventing postponed teardown execution.
expectation.conceptual: When pytest runs in --pdb mode, skipped unittest test classes must be treated identically to skipped individual test methods: their tearDown() must not execute. The skip check must account for skip decorators applied at both the class level and the method level.

constraints.grounded: The existing behavior for method-level skips under --pdb must remain unchanged. Tests that are not skipped (at either level) must continue to have their tearDown() postponed and executed as before when --pdb is active. The fix must only affect the tearDown postponement logic within TestCaseFunction and must not alter skip detection for non-pdb runs, which already work correctly.
constraints.conceptual: Normal (non-pdb) test execution behavior must not be affected. Method-level skip handling under --pdb must remain intact. Only the class-level skip gap in --pdb mode needs to be addressed. No other test lifecycle methods (e.g., setUp) should be impacted by this change.

behavior: When --pdb is active and a unittest.TestCase class is decorated with unittest.skip, tearDown() is no longer called for any test methods in that class.
When --pdb is active and a unittest.TestCase class is decorated with pytest.mark.skip, tearDown() is no longer called for any test methods in that class.
When --pdb is active and a test method (not the class) is decorated with unittest.skip or pytest.mark.skip, tearDown() is still correctly suppressed (existing behavior preserved).
When --pdb is active and neither the class nor the test method is skipped, tearDown() is still postponed and executed as before.
When --pdb is not active, class-level skipped tests continue to be skipped without executing tearDown() (existing behavior preserved).
acceptance_criteria: Given a unittest.TestCase class decorated with @unittest.skip, when pytest is run with --pdb, then tearDown() should NOT be executed for any test method in that class.
Given a unittest.TestCase class decorated with @pytest.mark.skip, when pytest is run with --pdb, then tearDown() should NOT be executed for any test method in that class.

Given a unittest.TestCase class that is NOT skipped but contains a method decorated with @unittest.skip, when pytest is run with --pdb, then tearDown() should NOT be executed for that skipped method (regression check for existing behavior).
Given a unittest.TestCase class that is NOT skipped with unskipped test methods, when pytest is run with --pdb, then tearDown() should still be postponed and executed normally after the test runs.

Given a unittest.TestCase class decorated with @unittest.skip, when pytest is run WITHOUT --pdb, then the tests should be reported as skipped and tearDown() should NOT be executed (no regression in non-pdb mode).

When a class-level skipped test is encountered under --pdb, no unexpected NameError or other tearDown-related error should surface, and PDB should not be entered due to tearDown failures on skipped tests.

task_2.title: Escape invalid XML characters in setup/teardown error messages for JUnit XML reports
task_2.description: Previously, when a test's setup or teardown phase produced error messages containing invalid XML characters (e.g., control characters or null bytes), the resulting JUnit XML report could contain malformed XML. This caused downstream XML parsers and CI systems consuming those reports to fail. The fix ensures that error messages from setup and teardown failures are properly XML-escaped before being written to the JUnit XML report, consistent with how other parts of the report already handle escaping.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that JUnit XML reports generated by pytest remain valid XML even when setup or teardown error messages contain characters that are invalid or special in XML (e.g., control characters, null bytes, or reserved XML entities). Previously, such characters in setup/teardown error messages were written unescaped into the report, producing malformed XML that could break downstream consumers such as CI dashboards and XML parsers.

expectation.grounded: When a test fails during setup or teardown and the error reason contains invalid XML characters, the _NodeReporter should apply bin_xml_escape to the error message string before passing it to _add_simple. The resulting 'error' element in the JUnit XML output must contain only valid, properly escaped XML content. This escaping must apply to the 'message' attribute of the error element specifically for setup and teardown failure paths.
expectation.conceptual: When generating JUnit XML reports, any error messages produced during the setup or teardown phases of a test must be sanitized so the output is always well-formed XML. Characters that are not permitted in XML documents should be escaped or replaced, ensuring that any XML parser can successfully consume the report regardless of what characters appear in the original error message.

constraints.grounded: The escaping must only affect the error message string (the 'msg' parameter) passed for setup/teardown failures, not the longrepr content which is already handled separately. The bin_xml_escape function must be used consistently for this message, matching the escaping strategy used elsewhere in the JUnit XML reporter. Existing escaping behavior for other report elements (test failure messages, skip reasons, xfail markers) must not be altered.
constraints.conceptual: The fix must not alter the semantic content of error messages beyond making them XML-safe. Other parts of the JUnit XML report generation that already handle escaping correctly must remain unchanged. The report must continue to distinguish between setup failures, teardown failures, and test body failures in its structure.

behavior: Setup failure error messages containing invalid XML characters are now escaped before inclusion in the JUnit XML error element.
Teardown failure error messages containing invalid XML characters are now escaped before inclusion in the JUnit XML error element.
The JUnit XML report output is always well-formed XML regardless of what characters appear in setup or teardown error reasons.
The escaping applies to the message attribute of the error element; the longrepr body content is unaffected by this change.
Characters such as control characters, null bytes, and other XML-illegal characters in error messages are replaced or escaped to produce valid XML.
acceptance_criteria: When a test fails on setup with an error reason containing a null byte character, the generated JUnit XML report should be parseable by a standard XML parser without errors.
When a test fails on teardown with an error reason containing XML-special characters (e.g., <, >, &), the generated JUnit XML error element message should contain properly escaped equivalents.

When a test fails on setup with an error reason containing control characters (e.g., \x0b, \x1b), those characters should be escaped or replaced in the JUnit XML output so the document remains valid XML.
When a test fails on setup or teardown with a plain ASCII error reason containing no special characters, the error message in the JUnit XML report should appear unchanged.
Existing JUnit XML output for test body failures, skips, and xfail markers should remain unaffected by this change.

task_4.title: Doctests now respect the --import-mode flag
task_4.description: The DoctestModule collector was not forwarding the user-configured --import-mode option when importing modules for doctest collection. This caused doctest modules to always be imported using the default import mode, ignoring the user's explicit configuration. As a result, namespace packages (PEP 420) with implicit namespaces could fail or be imported under incorrect module names when using --doctest-modules, because the import mode that properly supports namespace packages (e.g., importlib) was never applied. The fix ensures the configured import mode is passed through during doctest module import.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the --import-mode flag is respected when pytest collects and imports modules for doctest execution. Previously, running --doctest-modules with a non-default --import-mode (such as importlib) had no effect on how doctest modules were imported, causing failures with namespace packages that rely on the importlib import mode for correct module resolution. Modules could be imported under incorrect names or fail to resolve relative imports when the implicit namespace was missing from the import path.

expectation.grounded: When DoctestModule imports a module via import_path, it must pass the mode parameter derived from the --import-mode CLI option (via config.getoption('importmode')). This means specifying --import-mode=importlib should cause doctest module collection to use the importlib-based import strategy, and similarly for prepend or append modes. The import_path call in DoctestModule must behave identically to how other module collectors respect the import mode setting.
expectation.conceptual: Doctest module collection should honor the same --import-mode configuration that governs how all other test modules are imported. When a user sets --import-mode to a specific value, doctest modules must be imported using that same strategy, ensuring consistent module naming and namespace resolution across the entire test suite.

constraints.grounded: The existing error-handling behavior for ImportError in DoctestModule must be preserved: when doctest_ignore_import_errors is set, import failures should still result in a skip rather than a hard error. The default import mode behavior (when --import-mode is not explicitly set) must remain unchanged. The fix must only affect the import_path call within DoctestModule and not alter the import behavior of other collectors.
constraints.conceptual: The change must not break existing doctest collection for users who do not specify --import-mode. Import error handling and skip behavior for doctests must remain intact. The fix should bring doctest import behavior into alignment with the rest of pytest's module import infrastructure without introducing side effects.

behavior: When --import-mode=importlib is specified alongside --doctest-modules, doctest modules are now imported using the importlib-based strategy, enabling correct resolution of namespace packages.
When --import-mode=append or --import-mode=prepend is specified, doctest module collection uses the corresponding sys.path manipulation strategy during import.
Namespace packages with implicit namespaces no longer produce duplicate or misnamed module imports during doctest collection when the appropriate import mode is configured.
Relative imports within doctest modules now resolve correctly when --import-mode=importlib is used, because the module is imported under its fully qualified name including the namespace.
acceptance_criteria: When running pytest with --doctest-modules and --import-mode=importlib on a project containing namespace packages, doctest modules should be imported under their correct fully qualified module names without import errors.
When running pytest with --doctest-modules and --import-mode=prepend (default), doctest collection behavior should remain unchanged from prior versions.
When a doctest module fails to import and doctest_ignore_import_errors is enabled, the module should still be skipped gracefully regardless of the configured import mode.

When a package uses implicit namespace packages (PEP 420) and contains doctests with relative imports, running with --import-mode=importlib --doctest-modules should not produce ImportError or duplicate module name conflicts.

Given a project with a namespace package structure, when pytest is invoked with --doctest-modules --import-mode=importlib, then the collected doctest module's __name__ attribute should reflect the full dotted path including the namespace prefix.

task_5.title: Type-annotate FixtureRequest.param as Any for type-checker compatibility
task_5.description: Type checkers such as mypy reported 'FixtureRequest has no attribute param' when users accessed request.param inside parametrized fixtures, even though the attribute exists at runtime. This change declares param as a typed attribute (Any) on FixtureRequest so that type checkers recognize the attribute. It also adds type annotations to the internal helper get_direct_param_fixture_func. This is a stop-gap measure until a fuller generic typing solution (e.g., a ParametrizedFixtureRequest[T] class) is implemented.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that accessing `request.param` inside a parametrized fixture no longer triggers a type-checker error claiming 'FixtureRequest has no attribute param'. The `param` attribute is available at runtime for parametrized fixtures but was previously invisible to static analysis tools.

expectation.grounded: The `FixtureRequest` class must declare a `param` attribute typed as `Any`. After this change, mypy and other type checkers must not raise an attribute-error diagnostic when user code accesses `request.param` on a `FixtureRequest` (or `pytest.FixtureRequest`) typed parameter. The internal helper `get_direct_param_fixture_func` should also carry proper type annotations (accepting `FixtureRequest` and returning `Any`).
expectation.conceptual: When a user type-annotates a fixture's request parameter as `pytest.FixtureRequest` and accesses `request.param`, static type checkers should accept the code without reporting a missing-attribute error. The declared type of `param` should be `Any`, allowing any parameter value without narrowing.

constraints.grounded: The `param` attribute must remain `Any` rather than a more specific generic type, as the full generic solution (ParametrizedFixtureRequest[T]) is deferred. The attribute must be declared on `FixtureRequest` itself (not only on SubRequest) so that the common user-facing type annotation works. Runtime behavior of parametrized fixtures must not change — `request.param` must still raise `AttributeError` when accessed on a non-parametrized fixture request, preserving existing runtime semantics.
constraints.conceptual: This is a stop-gap typing improvement only; it must not alter runtime behavior of fixtures. The typing must be broad enough (Any) to avoid false positive type errors for any parameter type. Non-parametrized fixtures must continue to raise an error at runtime when param is accessed, even though the type annotation now declares the attribute.

behavior: FixtureRequest now declares a `param` attribute typed as `Any` during initialization, making it visible to static type checkers.
mypy and compatible type checkers no longer report 'FixtureRequest has no attribute param' when user code accesses `request.param`.
The internal function `get_direct_param_fixture_func` gains explicit type annotations (FixtureRequest -> Any), improving internal type safety.
Runtime behavior of parametrized and non-parametrized fixtures is unchanged — `request.param` still only holds a meaningful value for parametrized fixtures.
acceptance_criteria: When a fixture is declared with `params=[...]` and its argument is annotated as `pytest.FixtureRequest`, accessing `request.param` should produce no type-checker errors.

When running mypy (or an equivalent type checker) against code like `def myfixture(request: pytest.FixtureRequest) -> str: return request.param`, no 'has no attribute param' diagnostic should be emitted.
The inferred type of `request.param` should be `Any`, not a more restrictive type.
When a non-parametrized fixture accesses `request.param` at runtime, an `AttributeError` should still be raised, preserving existing runtime behavior.
Existing parametrized fixture tests must continue to pass without modification.

task_6.title: Fix AttributeError in assertion rewrite path handling when os.path is overridden
task_6.description: The path construction in AssertionRewritingHook._early_rewrite_bailout used os.path.sep to join module name parts into a path string. In certain environments—specifically when running tests in IDE debug mode (PyCharm, VS Code) with libraries that trigger deep import chains (e.g., geopandas via pyproj/certifi)—os.path could be replaced by a module variant (posixpath) lacking the sep attribute, causing an AttributeError and an INTERNALERROR crash during test collection. The fix replaces the os.path.sep-dependent path construction with PurePath's own API for assembling paths from parts, eliminating the dependency on os.path.sep entirely.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that pytest's assertion rewriting hook does not crash with an AttributeError during test collection when os.path has been replaced or overridden by an alternative module that lacks the 'sep' attribute. This occurs in specific environments such as IDE debug mode (PyCharm, VS Code) when third-party libraries trigger nested imports that re-enter the assertion rewriting import hook.

expectation.grounded: AssertionRewritingHook._early_rewrite_bailout must construct module-name-to-path mappings using PurePath's constructor and with_suffix API rather than relying on os.path.sep. The method should not raise AttributeError when os.path is substituted with a module lacking 'sep'. The early rewrite bailout logic must continue to correctly convert dotted module name parts into a PurePath with a .py suffix for pattern matching against fnpats.
expectation.conceptual: The assertion rewriting hook's early bailout path resolution must be robust against environments where the os.path module has been replaced or monkey-patched. Path construction from module name segments should use pathlib's native API to avoid any dependency on os.path attributes. The resulting path must remain functionally equivalent for subsequent filename pattern matching.

constraints.grounded: The path produced from module name parts must remain a valid PurePath with a .py suffix that correctly matches against the configured fnpats patterns. The fix must not change the semantics of how multi-part module names (containing subdirectory separators) are matched against patterns like 'tests/**.py'. No other behavior of AssertionRewritingHook.find_spec or _early_rewrite_bailout may be altered.
constraints.conceptual: The fix must preserve the existing pattern-matching behavior for assertion rewrite eligibility. Only the internal path construction mechanism should change; the observable result of which modules get rewritten and which bail out early must remain identical under normal conditions.

behavior: Previously, _early_rewrite_bailout raised AttributeError ('module posixpath has no attribute sep') when os.path was overridden during nested imports in certain environments. After the fix, path construction succeeds regardless of os.path's state.
PurePath(*parts).with_suffix('.py') produces an equivalent path to the previous os.path.sep-based construction under standard conditions, preserving correct module-to-path conversion.
The INTERNALERROR during pytest_collection that cascaded from the AttributeError in find_spec no longer occurs in IDE debug mode with libraries like geopandas.
Test collection and assertion rewriting proceed normally in debug and non-debug IDE modes when third-party libraries trigger re-entrant imports through the assertion rewriting meta path finder.
acceptance_criteria: When running pytest in IDE debug mode (e.g., PyCharm, VS Code) with a library like geopandas imported, test collection completes without INTERNALERROR or AttributeError.
When os.path is substituted with a module lacking the 'sep' attribute, AssertionRewritingHook._early_rewrite_bailout does not raise an AttributeError and returns a correct bailout decision.

When a dotted module name (e.g., 'package.submodule') is processed by _early_rewrite_bailout, the constructed PurePath correctly represents the module path with a .py suffix and matches against configured filename patterns identically to the previous behavior.
When assertion rewriting is configured with subdirectory patterns (e.g., 'tests/**.py'), the early bailout logic continues to correctly determine whether modules should be rewritten or skipped.
Normal (non-debug) test execution remains unaffected by the path construction change.

task_7.title: Fix pytest.approx string representation for tuple comparisons
task_7.description: When pytest.approx() was used to compare tuples (including tuples produced by ndarray.tolist()), the internal recursive mapping function only recognized list types, not tuples. This caused tuple elements to not be wrapped as ApproxScalar objects, leading to a TypeError ('object of type ApproxScalar has no len()') during representation, which surfaced as a faulty __repr__ message in assertion output. The fix generalizes the recursive mapping to handle both list and tuple sequences while preserving the original sequence type.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that pytest.approx() correctly produces its string representation when comparing tuples, including tuples of complex numbers. Previously, using pytest.approx() with tuple arguments caused a TypeError during assertion introspection, resulting in a 'faulty __repr__' error message instead of a clear diff of expected vs actual values.

expectation.grounded: The _recursive_sequence_map helper (formerly _recursive_list_map) must accept both list and tuple inputs and recursively apply the _approx_scalar wrapping to all elements. The return type must preserve the original sequence type (tuple in, tuple out; list in, list out). ApproxNumpy.__repr__ and ApproxNumpy._repr_compare must use this generalized mapping so that ndarray.tolist() results (which may contain tuples) are fully converted. ApproxSequenceLike._repr_compare must likewise use the generalized mapping to support tuple-based sequences.
expectation.conceptual: When pytest.approx() receives a tuple (or a nested structure containing tuples), it should produce a well-formed, human-readable string representation showing each element with its tolerance. The representation should work identically for tuples and lists, and should preserve the original container type in its output.

constraints.grounded: Existing behavior for list-based comparisons in ApproxNumpy and ApproxSequenceLike must remain unchanged. The recursive mapping must still correctly handle nested lists, nested tuples, and mixed list/tuple nesting. No new errors should be raised for numpy array comparisons whose tolist() produces lists.
constraints.conceptual: All existing pytest.approx() use cases involving lists, numpy arrays, and scalar values must continue to work without regressions. The fix must not alter comparison semantics—only the string representation path is affected.

behavior: The recursive mapping function now checks for both list and tuple types instead of only list
The return value of the recursive mapping preserves the original sequence type by capturing the input type and constructing the result with that type
ApproxNumpy.__repr__ correctly formats tuples returned by ndarray.tolist() by recursively wrapping all elements as ApproxScalar
ApproxNumpy._repr_compare correctly traverses tuple-based nested structures when computing per-element diffs
ApproxSequenceLike._repr_compare correctly maps over tuple-typed expected values when generating comparison output
No TypeError ('object of type ApproxScalar has no len()') is raised when representing tuple-based approximate comparisons
acceptance_criteria: When comparing two tuples using pytest.approx() (e.g., assert (1+0j, 2+0j) == pytest.approx((1, 2.2), abs=0.01)), the assertion failure message should display a clear 'approx(...)' representation showing each element with its tolerance, not a 'faulty __repr__' error
When comparing nested tuples using pytest.approx(), the representation should preserve the tuple structure and show tolerances for each scalar element
When comparing lists using pytest.approx(), the behavior and representation should remain identical to the previous version (no regression)
When comparing numpy arrays using pytest.approx(), the __repr__ and _repr_compare methods should work correctly regardless of whether ndarray.tolist() returns lists or tuples
The recursive mapping function should preserve the original container type: given a tuple input it should return a tuple, and given a list input it should return a list

task_8.title: Add explicit deprecation notes to tmpdir and tmpdir_factory fixture docstrings
task_8.description: The legacy tmpdir and tmpdir_factory fixtures lacked prominent deprecation guidance in their docstrings. Users consulting the API reference could easily miss that tmp_path and tmp_path_factory are the preferred replacements. This change adds visible note admonitions to the TempdirFactory class, the tmpdir fixture, and related methods, directing users toward the modern tmp_path-based alternatives. Additionally, docstring cross-references were corrected to point to public API names (py.path.local, TempPathFactory) instead of internal identifiers.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the docstrings for the legacy tmpdir fixture and tmpdir_factory (including the TempdirFactory class and its methods mktemp and getbasetemp) contain explicit, prominent notes advising users to prefer tmp_path and tmp_path_factory respectively. Ensure that all type references in these docstrings refer to the public py.path.local type and TempPathFactory class rather than internal module paths.

expectation.grounded: The TempdirFactory class docstring must include a note admonition stating that tmp_path_factory is preferred, with a cross-reference to the 'tmpdir and tmpdir_factory' documentation section. The tmpdir fixture docstring in LegacyTmpdirPlugin must include a note admonition stating that tmp_path is preferred, with the same cross-reference. TempdirFactory.mktemp and TempdirFactory.getbasetemp docstrings must reference py.path.local as the return type and reference TempPathFactory methods. The TempdirFactory class docstring must use correct single-backtick RST :class: role syntax for py.path.local and TempPathFactory.
expectation.conceptual: All legacy temporary directory fixtures and their factory class must carry prominent deprecation-style notes directing users to the modern tmp_path and tmp_path_factory equivalents. Method docstrings must reference the public return type and the corresponding modern factory methods rather than internal implementation details.

constraints.grounded: No runtime behavior, function signatures, or return values of tmpdir, tmpdir_factory, TempdirFactory.mktemp, or TempdirFactory.getbasetemp may change. The note admonitions must use RST .. note:: directive syntax. Cross-references to documentation sections must use :ref: roles. Type references must use :class: roles with correct single-backtick syntax.
constraints.conceptual: This change must be purely documentation-level with no effect on runtime behavior. The deprecation guidance must be informational (not a warning or error at runtime). Existing fixture functionality must remain fully intact and backward-compatible.

behavior: The rendered API documentation for the TempdirFactory class now displays a prominent note recommending tmp_path_factory as the preferred alternative.
The rendered API documentation for the tmpdir fixture now displays a prominent note recommending tmp_path as the preferred alternative.
The TempdirFactory.mktemp docstring now describes its return type as py.path.local instead of referencing the internal _pytest.compat.LEGACY_PATH alias.
The TempdirFactory.getbasetemp docstring now mirrors the mktemp description pattern, describing itself relative to TempPathFactory.getbasetemp and documenting its py.path.local return type.
The TempdirFactory class docstring RST markup is corrected from double-backtick :class: references to proper single-backtick syntax, fixing rendering in generated documentation.
acceptance_criteria: When a user views the TempdirFactory class docstring (via help() or generated docs), they see a note stating that tmp_path_factory is preferred, with a reference to the tmpdir and tmpdir_factory documentation section.
When a user views the tmpdir fixture docstring, they see a note stating that tmp_path is preferred, with a reference to the tmpdir and tmpdir_factory documentation section.
When a user views the TempdirFactory.mktemp docstring, the return type is described as py.path.local, not as an internal _pytest.compat type.
When a user views the TempdirFactory.getbasetemp docstring, it describes the method relative to TempPathFactory.getbasetemp and documents the py.path.local return type.
When the documentation is built, all :class: and :meth: cross-references in the modified docstrings resolve correctly without Sphinx warnings.
No existing tests fail and runtime behavior of tmpdir, tmpdir_factory, TempdirFactory.mktemp, and TempdirFactory.getbasetemp remains unchanged.

task_9.title: Replace atomicwrites dependency with os.replace for pyc cache writing
task_9.description: The third-party atomicwrites library, previously used on Windows for atomic .pyc cache file writes during assertion rewriting, was removed as a dependency after the library was declared unmaintained by its author. The platform-conditional code paths (one for Windows using atomicwrites, one for other platforms using os.rename) were unified into a single cross-platform implementation that writes to a temporary PID-suffixed file and then uses os.replace to atomically move it to the target path. os.replace provides correct atomic overwrite semantics on all platforms including Windows, where os.rename cannot overwrite existing files.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the atomicwrites third-party dependency is removed and that .pyc assertion-rewrite cache files are still written atomically on all platforms, including Windows, using only standard library facilities. The previous dependency was declared unmaintained and removed from PyPI, making it an unreliable supply-chain component for a critical project like pytest.

expectation.grounded: The _write_pyc function in the assertion rewrite module should use a single, platform-independent implementation. It should write compiled code to a temporary file (PID-suffixed), then atomically move it to the final .pyc path using os.replace. On success it returns True; on any OSError during writing or replacing it logs the error via state.trace and returns False. The atomicwrites package must no longer be imported or required as a dependency.
expectation.conceptual: When pytest rewrites assertion bytecode and caches the compiled .pyc file, the write operation must be atomic on all supported platforms. A temporary file is written first, then atomically moved to the target location. If any filesystem error occurs during writing or moving, the operation fails gracefully without raising exceptions to the caller. No third-party library is required for this functionality.

constraints.grounded: The atomicwrites package must not appear in any import statement or dependency specification. os.replace must be used instead of os.rename for the atomic move step, because os.rename does not support overwriting existing files on Windows. The temporary file must be uniquely named per process (PID-suffixed) to avoid conflicts in concurrent test runs. OSError during file creation or atomic replacement must be caught separately and traced, returning False without propagating the exception.
constraints.conceptual: No unmaintained or removed third-party packages may be used for file atomicity. The cache write mechanism must work correctly on all platforms including Windows, must handle concurrent process access safely, and must degrade gracefully on filesystem errors without crashing the test session.

behavior: The _write_pyc function is now a single implementation used on all platforms, removing the previous sys.platform == 'win32' conditional branching.
On Windows, the atomicwrites.atomic_write call is replaced by writing to a PID-suffixed temporary file followed by os.replace, which supports atomic overwrite on Windows.
On non-Windows platforms, os.rename is replaced by os.replace, which has equivalent behavior on POSIX but provides consistent cross-platform semantics.
The file handle is now managed via a with-statement context manager instead of manual try/finally/close.
The atomicwrites package is completely removed as an import and dependency.
Error handling preserves the same observable behavior: OSError during write or replace is traced and causes _write_pyc to return False.
acceptance_criteria: When pytest performs assertion rewriting and writes a .pyc cache file on Windows, the write succeeds atomically without requiring the atomicwrites package.
When pytest performs assertion rewriting and writes a .pyc cache file on non-Windows platforms, the write succeeds atomically using os.replace.
When the .pyc target file already exists, os.replace overwrites it atomically on all platforms, including Windows.
When a filesystem error occurs during writing to the temporary file, _write_pyc returns False and traces the error including errno.
When a filesystem error occurs during the os.replace step, _write_pyc returns False and traces the error.
When multiple pytest processes run concurrently, each writes to a unique PID-suffixed temporary file, preventing conflicts.
The atomicwrites package is not imported anywhere and is not listed as a dependency.
